name: Expense Fraud
title: Expense Fraud
answer: Expense fraud covers claims that are false, inflated, duplicated or outside policy, from a fabricated taxi receipt to a supplier invoice routed through an employee's own account. In an AI accounting context it sits inside fraud detection and forensics, alongside procurement fraud, payroll fraud and vendor collusion. The work spans the whole claim lifecycle: submission, approval, reimbursement and the later audit that finds what the first three missed. It is a control problem as much as a detection problem, because most losses come from claims that were approved by a person who had no reason to look closely.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Expense fraud covers claims that are false, inflated, duplicated or outside policy, from a fabricated taxi receipt to a supplier invoice routed through an employee's own account. In an AI accounting context it sits inside fraud detection and forensics, alongside procurement fraud, payroll fraud and vendor collusion. The work spans the whole claim lifecycle: submission, approval, reimbursement and the later audit that finds what the first three missed. It is a control problem as much as a detection problem, because most losses come from claims that were approved by a person who had no reason to look closely.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Detection runs on the accounting and expense systems that already hold the data: the expense platform, the corporate card feed, the purchase ledger and the HR record that shows who reports to whom. Analysts add a rules layer for hard limits and a model layer for patterns that rules miss, such as a claimant whose spending drifts just under an approval threshold. Receipt images and email approvals are pulled in where optical character recognition and text extraction can turn them into comparable fields. The output usually lands in a case management queue rather than straight into a payment block, so a human decides what happens next.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The practical method is triage: score every claim, rank it, and send only the top slice to an investigator. Rules catch the obvious, duplicate receipts, weekend claims from staff who were not travelling, amounts split to stay under a limit. Models catch the relational signals, an employee and a vendor sharing an address, a manager approving every claim from one team without exception, a merchant that appears only in one person's expenses. Investigators then work the case with documents, interviews and bank records, and the finding is written up so it can survive an internal review or an external challenge. Feedback from closed cases is what keeps the scoring honest over time.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Expense data is personal data, so collection, retention and access all need a stated basis, and monitoring staff spending carries works council or employee representative issues in many jurisdictions. Findings that lead to dismissal or prosecution have to be evidenced to an employment or criminal standard, not just a model score, which is why case files matter more than alerts. Provenance of the evidence chain, who saw what, when, and from which system, is what makes a finding defensible. The site tracks 229 compliance and regulation pages and 150 active AI lawsuits, a reminder that automated decisions about people attract scrutiny. Any use of a model in this area should be documented, reviewable and open to challenge by the person accused.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward continuous monitoring rather than periodic audit, with scores refreshed as claims arrive instead of reviewed once a quarter. Expect tighter coupling between expense tools and card networks, so a claim can be checked against the transaction at the moment it is filed. Generative tools will make fabricated receipts cheaper to produce, which pushes detection toward source verification rather than document appearance. The harder problem is not detection but proportionate response, since a system that flags too many honest claims will be switched off by the people it was meant to help. Smaller finance teams will feel this most, because they carry the same control obligations without a forensic unit to fall back on.
